subject: physics
title: Brownian motion
key_idea: Tiny specks in air or water jiggle about at random when seen through a microscope. They are knocked by fast, light molecules that are too small to see. This is evidence that matter is made of particles in constant random motion.

blocks.text: Brownian motion is the random movement of microscopic particles. You can see it with a microscope, but only in a liquid or a gas.

items.meaning: The continuous, random movement of microscopic particles in a fluid.
Tiny solid particles spread through a liquid or a gas.

items: Smoke particles in air, seen as bright specks, move in a jerky, zigzag path.
Pollen grains in water move continually and randomly.
The particles do not all move in the same direction, and their path keeps changing.
Microscopic particles in a liquid or gas move continually and randomly.

blocks.text: The air or water is made of molecules that are far too small to see. They are always moving, and they collide with the visible particle.

items.text: The molecules of air or water move quickly in random directions.
They collide with the microscopic particle from all sides.
At any moment there are more collisions on one side than on the other.
The unbalanced force pushes the particle a tiny distance in one direction.
The imbalance keeps changing direction, so the path is random.

diagram.alt: A sequencing activity. Put the steps that make a smoke particle move randomly in the correct order.
diagram.prompt: Put these steps in order to explain why a smoke particle moves.
steps: Air molecules move quickly in random directions.
The air molecules collide with the smoke particle.
More molecules hit one side of the particle than the other.
The unbalanced force pushes the particle a tiny distance.
The imbalance changes direction, so the path is random.

items: The molecules are **light** and **fast-moving**, so their collisions can move the much heavier particle.
Brownian motion is **evidence** for the kinetic particle model. It shows that the molecules exist and are in constant random motion.
Random collisions with fast molecules cause the motion.
It is evidence that matter is made of moving particles.

blocks.text: (Supplement) Use the words carefully. What you see is not a molecule.

items: A **microscopic particle** such as smoke or pollen is large enough to see with a microscope. It is made of a huge number of atoms or molecules.
A **molecule** or atom, such as nitrogen or water, is far too small to see.
Each molecule is far lighter than the particle, so one collision moves the particle only a tiny amount.

diagram.alt: A sorting activity. Sort each item into microscopic particles seen under a microscope, and molecules too small to see.
diagram.prompt: Is each one a microscopic particle you can see with a microscope, or a molecule you cannot?

items: Smoke and pollen are microscopic particles, not molecules.
Light, fast-moving molecules knock the microscopic particles about.

checks.q: Describe the motion of pollen grains in water seen through a microscope.
checks.a: They move continually and randomly, in a jerky, zigzag path.

checks.q: Explain why a smoke particle in air moves randomly.
checks.a: Fast-moving air molecules hit it at random from all sides. The collisions on each side are unbalanced at any moment, and the imbalance keeps changing direction.

checks.q: (Supplement) State why Brownian motion is evidence for the particle model of matter.
checks.a: It shows that molecules too small to see are moving randomly and colliding with the visible particles.
